meta.title: Who really said "When life gives you lemons, make lemonade"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dale Carnegie popularized it in 1948 but credited Julius Rosenwald. Quote Investigator traces the adage to an anonymous 1907 newspaper verse.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When life gives you lemons, make lemonade'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Carnegie's line. He credited Sears president Julius Rosenwald in 1948 — and the adage was already in print, anonymously, in 1907.

answer.label: Not Dale Carnegie — an anonymous proverb he helped popularize
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented May 1907 · anonymous verse in a Montana newspaper
answer.sourceLine: Dale Carnegie did put a version of this adage into a bestseller — chapter 17 of How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) is titled “If You Have a Lemon, Make a Lemonade” — but he explicitly did not claim it, crediting Sears president Julius Rosenwald by way of University of Chicago chancellor Robert Maynard Hutchins. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying back to an anonymous 1907 newspaper verse and concludes the originator remains anonymous; the exact modern wording turns up in its survey only in 1971, on an unattributed bumper sticker.

source.heading: The earliest documented ancestor

docMeta.dd: “When life gives you lemons, make lemonade”
The Kalispell Bee, Montana, May 1907 — anonymous verse
Dale Carnegie, How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948), ch. 17
Unattributed bumper sticker, printed in a Buffalo, New York newspaper, October 1971

source.excerpt: Turn failure into victory, / Don’t let your courage fade; / And if you get a lemon, why / Just make the lemonade.
trail: May 1907 — the earliest appearance Quote Investigator ↗ documents: an anonymous four-line verse in The Kalispell Bee of Montana ending “And if you get a lemon, why / Just make the lemonade.” No author is named. By December 1907 a Biddeford, Maine paper was running its own version.
July 1908 — Elbert Hubbard prints a memorable variant in The Philistine: “He is a great man who accepts the lemons that Fate passes out to him and uses them to start a lemonade stand.”

February 1915 — a later, better-travelled Hubbard wording appears in his obituary of the actor Marshall Pinckney Wilder (“The King of Jesters,” The Fra, February 1915): “He picked up the lemons that Fate had sent him and started a lemonade-stand.” Wikiquote ↗ cites it to the posthumous collection Selected Writings of Elbert Hubbard (1922), p. 237, seven years after Hubbard wrote it.

1948 — Dale Carnegie gives the adage its mass audience as the title of chapter 17 of How to Stop Worrying and Start Living ↗: “If You Have a Lemon, Make a Lemonade.” In the chapter he credits Julius Rosenwald, quoting chancellor Robert Maynard Hutchins’s version: “When you have a lemon, make a lemonade.”

October 1971 — the exact modern wording surfaces in QI’s survey ↗, and it surfaces anonymously: a Buffalo, New York newspaper reprints the text of a batch of bumper stickers, among them “When Life Gives You Lemons, Make Lemonade.”
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest documented ancestor of the saying, not the modern wording — the anonymous four-line verse that Quote Investigator ↗ identifies as the first appearance in print. By December 1907 a Maine paper was already defining an optimist as “a man who can make lemonade out of all the lemons handed him.”

artifact.kindLabel: The popularizer’s book — not the origin
artifact.linkText: Dale Carnegie, How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (Simon and Schuster, 1948) on the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording, because no author or first publication has been identified for it — the earliest instance in the specialist research is an unattributed 1971 bumper sticker. The separate texts around it have clear statuses: the anonymous May 1907 newspaper verse is long out of copyright, while Dale Carnegie’s How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (Simon and Schuster, 1948) remains in copyright, which is why the Internet Archive lends rather than freely serves it.

author.name: Dale Carnegie
author.heading: Why the credit landed on Dale Carnegie
author.bio: Dale Carnegie was born on a Missouri farm in 1888 and built a career teaching public speaking and interpersonal skills, beginning with a YMCA course in 1912. His two great bestsellers, How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) and How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948), made him the founding figure of the modern self-help shelf. The lemonade adage attached itself to his name because the 1948 book gave it a chapter heading and a mass audience — but Carnegie was reporting the line, not coining it, and he named someone else as its source.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented form: anonymous verse, The Kalispell Bee (Kalispell, MT), May 1907. Popularized as chapter 17, “If You Have a Lemon, Make a Lemonade,” in Dale Carnegie, How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (New York: Simon and Schuster, 1948). The exact modern wording appears in Quote Investigator's survey as an unattributed bumper sticker printed in a Buffalo, New York newspaper, October 1971. See “Quote Origin: If Life Gives You Lemons, Make Lemonade,” Quote Investigator, April 4, 2024.

copyAttribution: Anonymous proverb — the adage is in print by May 1907 (The Kalispell Bee, Montana); this exact wording is first documented, unattributed, in 1971. Not Dale Carnegie, who printed a variant as a chapter title in "How to Stop Worrying and Start Living" (1948) and credited Julius Rosenwald. Verified via Quote Investigator. Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This adage has collected credits the way few sayings do — and the specialist research clears all three of the usual candidates.

items.why: Carnegie titled chapter 17 of How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) “If You Have a Lemon, Make a Lemonade” — not the modern wording — and in the text he attributes the advice to someone else entirely, writing that chancellor Robert Maynard Hutchins told him he followed “a bit of advice given to me by the late Julius Rosenwald.” Quote Investigator ↗ notes that Carnegie thereby disclaimed credit.

Hubbard (1856–1915, the Roycroft founder who died on the Lusitania) wrote in The Philistine in July 1908: “He is a great man who accepts the lemons that Fate passes out to him and uses them to start a lemonade stand.” QI ↗ dates that after the anonymous 1907 verse and calls it a statement in the same family rather than the origin. A 1944 Pennsylvania newspaper went further and credited Hubbard with a reworded version: “When life hands you a lemon, add some sugar and make lemonade.”

items.tag: undated and reported at one remove
items.why: Carnegie's credit reaches Rosenwald only through Hutchins's recollection, with no date attached, in the form “When you have a lemon, make a lemonade.” Rosenwald (1862–1932) was a Sears, Roebuck ↗ executive from 1895 — vice-president and treasurer through 1907 — and its president from 1908. Quote Investigator ↗ records Carnegie's credit without dating or confirming it, and concludes the originator is anonymous.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody owns this one: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the adage was circulating by 1907 and “the originator remains anonymous.”

context.heading: Why a lemon?
lead: The joke only works because of a piece of forgotten slang. In early-1900s American English, to be handed a lemon meant to be palmed off with something worthless or to be dealt a bad turn — a lemon was anything shoddy or disappointing, a sense that survives today mainly in “lemon” for a defective car. Quote Investigator ↗ documents that slang as the soil the adage grew in.

Once that idiom existed, the comeback wrote itself, and it wrote itself many times over. The 1907 verse says “if you get a lemon”; Elbert Hubbard's 1908 version has Fate passing out the lemons; Carnegie's 1948 chapter says “if you have a lemon.” The crisp modern form — life gives you lemons — is the survivor of that long shaking-out, and it has no author's name on it.
context.detailsSummary: How a proverb gets a famous author
detailsBody: Anonymous sayings are unstable: they drift in wording and they drift in attribution. Both kinds of drift are visible here. A 1944 Pennsylvania newspaper credited Elbert Hubbard with a wording he is not documented as having written, and by the late twentieth century the whole adage had been reassigned to Dale Carnegie, whose book had given it its widest airing.
This is the ordinary life cycle of a proverb in the attribution economy: a line with no author is uncomfortable, so it acquires one — usually the most famous name standing nearby.
context.pull: A lemon meant a raw deal. The proverb is a pun that outlived its own slang.
